name: Quantum Gravimeters
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Finding Hidden Tunnels by Weighing Nothing
lesson.summary: Quantum gravimeters use free-falling clouds of laser-cooled atoms to measure gravitational acceleration precisely enough to detect underground voids and buried infrastructure, building on the same atom-cooling techniques used in atomic clocks.
lesson.body:
Gravity is the weakest of the fundamental forces, but it is also relentlessly informative: the strength of the gravitational pull at any point on Earth's surface depends on the density of everything beneath it. A cavity, a tunnel, an ore deposit, or a shift in magma all change the local density enough to produce a tiny but measurable change in the local value of g, the acceleration due to gravity. Classical gravimeters have measured this for decades using a falling mass and a spring or laser interferometer. Quantum gravimeters replace the mass with a cloud of atoms cooled to near absolute zero, and replace the spring with the wave nature of matter itself.

The technique is called atom interferometry, and it borrows directly from the laser cooling and trapping methods developed for atomic clocks. A cloud of atoms, often rubidium, is laser cooled into a tight ball and then released into free fall. A precisely timed sequence of laser pulses splits each atom's quantum wavefunction into a superposition of two paths that separate slightly and then recombine, in the same conceptual way light splits and recombines in an optical interferometer. Because the two paths experience gravity along slightly different trajectories, they pick up a phase difference when they recombine, and that phase difference is a direct, extremely precise readout of local gravitational acceleration.

The precision on offer is remarkable. Modern quantum gravimeters can resolve changes in g at the level of a few parts in a billion, sensitive enough to detect a human sized void several meters underground. That has real commercial uses. Utility companies use quantum gravimeters to map buried pipes and tunnels without digging exploratory trenches, geotechnical engineers use them to find sinkhole risk before a road or building goes in, and oil and mineral exploration companies use them as a faster, sometimes cheaper complement to seismic surveys for narrowing down where to drill or dig next. Volcanologists use continuously operating gravimeters to track the slow movement of magma beneath a volcano, which shows up as a gradual change in the local mass distribution.

As with magnetometers, notice what a gravimeter is not doing. It is not running an algorithm, storing quantum information across many entangled qubits, or performing error corrected logic gates. It is exploiting the interference of a single cloud of identical atoms to make one exceptionally precise measurement of one physical quantity. That focus, one well understood measurement rather than an open ended computation, is exactly why gravimeters, magnetometers, and atomic clocks have reached commercial deployment years, in some cases decades, ahead of general purpose quantum computers.
